title: Learning Theory Matrix
note: The four theories and four dimensions are invented for this exercise. They are simplified composites, not published theories.

emphasisLegend.high: central concern of the theory on this dimension
emphasisLegend.unique: a feature no other theory in the table has

learnerRole.description: The learner is the center of this theory. Progress comes from trying things, noticing patterns and forming a rule, not from being told the rule first.
learnerRole.example: In a bouncing-ball MicroSim, the learner changes gravity several times and discovers that a stronger pull makes each bounce shorter.

simRole.description: Only this theory treats the MicroSim as an open space with no required order of steps. Every control is available from the start.
simRole.example: A pendulum lab opens with every slider unlocked and a single question: what changes how fast the pendulum swings?

evidence.description: Evidence matters, but it is gathered informally at the end, when the learner can state the rule they found in their own words.
evidence.example: After exploring, the learner types 'a longer string gives a slower swing' into a short text box.

feedback.description: Feedback is held back so that it does not cut discovery short. The theory gives it little weight while the activity is running.
feedback.example: The MicroSim reveals the accepted rule only after the learner has submitted their own.

learnerRole.description: The learner follows a schedule set by the system. Choosing what to study or how to explore gets little attention in this model.
learnerRole.example: Each morning the learner answers the ten items the MicroSim has scheduled for review, in the order given.

simRole.description: The MicroSim does the central work: it decides which item to show next and when to show it again, based on past answers.
simRole.example: A flashcard MicroSim shows a missed chart-type question again after one day, then after three days, then after a week.

evidence.description: Only this model measures learning by testing the same item again after days have passed, to check that it is retained and not just recognized.
evidence.example: The MicroSim reports that the learner still answers 8 of 10 items correctly one week after first learning them.

feedback.description: Right-or-wrong feedback after every answer is a core part of the model, because each answer updates the review schedule.
feedback.example: A green check or a red cross with the correct answer appears the moment the learner submits each card.

learnerRole.description: The learner explains ideas to others and listens to their explanations, and the approach weights both roles equally.
learnerRole.example: Pairs take turns: one learner explains why a pie chart fails for eight categories, then the other restates the explanation and adds an example.

simRole.description: The MicroSim matters little here. It supplies a common thing to look at, and the learning happens in the conversation around it.
simRole.example: The whole group looks at one priority-matrix MicroSim projected on a screen while discussing where each item belongs.

evidence.description: Evidence comes from how well learners explain and justify ideas, but it is judged loosely, as one part of the discussion.
evidence.example: The instructor notes which learners can explain why an item moved from Quick Wins to Major Projects.

feedback.description: Only this approach relies on other learners, not the MicroSim or an instructor, as the main source of feedback.
feedback.example: A partner points out that the learner's flowchart has no path back from the No branch, and they fix it together.

rows.name: Tuned Challenge Model
rows.subtitle: learning at the edge of skill

learnerRole.value: Works at the edge of skill
learnerRole.description: The learner is expected to stretch just beyond what they can already do, but the model focuses more on the system than on the learner's choices.
learnerRole.example: A learner who solves three function-matching tasks in a row is given one that needs two steps instead of one.

simRole.description: Only this model has the MicroSim change its own difficulty while the learner works, based on recent performance.
simRole.example: After two wrong answers, a slope MicroSim switches from fractional slopes back to whole-number slopes.

evidence.description: Evidence combines how often the learner is right with how quickly they answer, and the model weights the two equally.
evidence.example: The MicroSim raises the level only when the learner is at least 80 percent correct and answers within 20 seconds.

feedback.description: Immediate feedback is central, because each result decides the difficulty of the next task.
feedback.example: A correct answer shows 'Level up: next task has two unknowns' before the next task loads.
